title: AI Unlocked: Politics & Governance
blurb: For campaigners, public servants, and civic organizations: policy analysis at speed, constituent communication, campaign operations, disinformation defense, and the ethics/regulation landscape shaping AI in public life.

modules.t: AI in Public Life: The Map
modules.d: How AI is entering government, parliaments, campaigns and civil society — and the democratic values at stake.
modules.body:
Why public life is different

When businesses adopt AI, the main stakes are efficiency and competitiveness. In public life, the stakes include rights, trust and democratic legitimacy. A government chatbot that gives wrong benefit information, an algorithm that unfairly flags citizens for investigation, or a deepfake released days before an election can harm individuals and erode trust in institutions. Public servants, elected officials, campaigners and civic organisations therefore carry special responsibilities when using AI.

The landscape

  • Government and public administration: drafting documents, summarising consultations, answering citizen enquiries, translating services, analysing data for planning, fraud detection and case management.
  • Parliaments and legislatures: summarising bills and amendments, comparing laws across jurisdictions, analysing public submissions and supporting committee research.
  • Political campaigns and parties: message drafting, voter outreach, volunteer coordination, fundraising communications and opposition research.
  • Civil society and advocacy: policy analysis, campaign materials, monitoring of government performance and elections, and fact-checking.
  • Media and information ecosystems: AI-generated content, recommendation algorithms and synthetic media that shape what citizens see.

Democratic values as a lens

Evaluate any AI use in public life against core democratic values: legality (lawful authority and compliance), accountability (identifiable humans answerable for decisions), transparency (people know when and how AI is used in decisions affecting them), equality and non-discrimination, privacy, participation (citizens can be heard and contest decisions), and truthfulness in public communication. The OECD AI Principles and UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of AI articulate similar values internationally.

Cautionary cases. In the Netherlands, a childcare benefits scandal involving risk-scoring and discriminatory practices wrongly accused thousands of families of fraud, contributing to the government's resignation in 2021. In Australia, the automated "Robodebt" debt-recovery scheme was found unlawful and the subject of a Royal Commission in 2023. Both show how automated decision-making without legality, fairness and human accountability can cause serious harm to citizens.

Regulation is developing

The European Union's AI Act classifies several public-sector uses — such as access to essential public services and benefits, law enforcement and migration — and AI systems intended to influence elections or voting behaviour, as high-risk, with obligations for risk management, transparency and human oversight. The EU has also adopted rules on the transparency and targeting of political advertising. Many countries are developing national AI strategies and laws, and data protection laws apply widely, including across Africa. Political actors must know the rules in every jurisdiction where they operate.

Neutrality of this course

This course is non-partisan. Its methods apply equally to governments and oppositions, parties of any orientation, and civic organisations of any cause. The common standard is lawful, truthful, accountable and fair use of AI in public life.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my public-sector AI advisor. Ask me whether I work in government, a legislature, a campaign or civil society, and my country. Map the AI uses relevant to my role, evaluate each against legality, accountability, transparency, equality, privacy, participation and truthfulness, and identify which uses would likely be high-risk under frameworks such as the EU AI Act. Remind me to verify the current laws in my jurisdiction.

📚 Glossary

  • Automated decision-making: decisions made by systems with little or no human involvement
  • High-risk AI: EU AI Act category requiring strict obligations
  • Democratic legitimacy: public acceptance that authority is exercised rightfully
  • Synthetic media: AI-generated or manipulated audio, images or video

📖 References

  • OECD (2019, updated 2024). Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence.
  • UNESCO (2021). Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence.
  • European Union — Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), Annex III.
  • Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme (Australia, 2023), Final Report.
  • Dutch Parliamentary Inquiry into the childcare benefits affair (2020).

quiz.q: A ministry wants to deploy an algorithm that automatically flags benefit recipients for fraud investigation and suspends payments. Which lesson from the Dutch and Australian cases is MOST relevant?
opts: Automated decisions affecting citizens require legality, fairness testing, human accountability and the ability to contest decisions
Suspensions are acceptable if the algorithm is accurate on average
quiz.x: Both scandals involved harmful automated or semi-automated decisions lacking safeguards.

quiz.q: Which democratic value is MOST directly at stake when citizens are not told that an AI system influenced a decision about them?
quiz.x: People should know when AI is used in decisions affecting them.

quiz.q: Under the EU AI Act, how are AI systems intended to influence elections or voting behaviour classified?
quiz.x: They are listed among high-risk uses with corresponding obligations.

quiz.q: A parliamentary research unit uses AI to summarise 5,000 public submissions on a bill. Which safeguard BEST protects participation?
opts: Summarise only submissions from large organisations
Validate the summary with human review, check minority views are represented, and keep original submissions available
quiz.x: Participation requires that all voices are fairly represented and verifiable.

quiz.q: Why does the course describe public-sector AI stakes as different from business AI?
opts: Public decisions affect rights, trust and democratic legitimacy, not only efficiency
quiz.x: The consequences touch citizens' rights and institutional trust.

quiz.q: Which statement BEST describes this course's political stance?
opts: It is non-partisan, applying the same standards of lawful, truthful, accountable and fair AI use to all actors
quiz.x: The methods and standards apply equally to all political actors.

quiz.q: A city deploys an AI chatbot for residents' tax questions without checking answers against current law. What is the MAIN risk?
opts: Residents receiving wrong information and acting on it, harming them and trust
quiz.x: Inaccurate public information harms citizens and institutional credibility.

quiz.q: Which framework articulates international principles for trustworthy AI adopted by many governments?
quiz.x: The OECD Recommendation on AI is widely endorsed.

quiz.q: A civic organisation uses AI to monitor government budget execution. Which value should guide its published findings?
quiz.x: Credibility depends on accurate, verifiable findings.

quiz.q: Which group should be identifiable and answerable for an AI-supported public decision?
quiz.x: Accountability requires identifiable humans responsible for decisions.

modules.d: Using AI to research, compare and draft policy — with evidence, balance and verification.
modules.body:
The policy cycle

Public policy typically moves through agenda setting (defining the problem), formulation (developing options), decision (adoption by authorised bodies), implementation and evaluation. AI can accelerate research and drafting at each stage — but policy quality depends on evidence, stakeholder insight and judgement about values and trade-offs, which remain human responsibilities.

Problem definition and evidence

Strong policy begins with a precise problem statement supported by data: who is affected, how much, where and why. AI can help structure the problem, suggest causes and identify data sources, but statistics must come from verifiable sources such as national statistics institutes, administrative data, peer-reviewed research and reputable international organisations. Generative AI can fabricate statistics and citations; every figure in a policy paper must be traced to its source.

Comparative policy research

Policymakers often ask how other countries have addressed similar problems. AI can quickly outline approaches and point to examples, but laws, institutions and contexts differ. Verify each example in primary sources (official legislation, government reports, evaluations) and assess transferability: Does the context resemble yours in institutions, capacity, culture and resources? What evidence shows it worked, and for whom?

Options analysis. Good policy advice presents several realistic options — including doing nothing or improving existing measures — and assesses each against explicit criteria: effectiveness, cost, equity, feasibility, legal compliance, political acceptability and risks. AI can draft an options matrix from your inputs; you supply the evidence and weigh the trade-offs.

Regulatory impact assessment

Many governments use regulatory impact assessment (RIA) to analyse the expected benefits, costs and distributional effects of proposed rules before adoption, with consultation of affected parties. AI can help structure an RIA, summarise consultation responses and draft sections — while economists, legal experts and stakeholders provide the analysis and validation.

Legislative drafting and analysis

AI can summarise bills, compare versions and amendments, identify affected existing laws, translate between official languages, and draft explanatory notes in plain language. Legal drafting itself requires qualified legislative drafters: precision of terms, consistency with the constitution and existing law, enforceability, and the jurisdiction's drafting conventions. In bilingual systems such as Cameroon's (English and French), both language versions must be consistent and legally equivalent.

Balanced analysis

AI outputs can reflect biases in their training data and in how questions are framed. Ask for the strongest arguments for and against each option, the interests of different stakeholder groups, and evidence that challenges your preferred position. Analysts who serve the public have a duty to present evidence honestly, even when it is politically inconvenient.

Stakeholder mapping

Policies succeed or fail with stakeholders — citizens, businesses, civil society, implementing agencies, local authorities, unions and international partners. AI can draft stakeholder maps and anticipate concerns; genuine consultation, especially with affected and marginalised groups, cannot be simulated.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my policy analyst. I will describe a policy problem and my country context. Help me write a precise problem statement, list the evidence I need and where to find it, outline approaches used elsewhere (marked for verification in primary sources), and build an options matrix including the status quo, assessed on effectiveness, cost, equity, feasibility, legal compliance, political acceptability and risk. Present the strongest arguments for and against each option.

📚 Glossary

  • Policy cycle: agenda setting, formulation, decision, implementation, evaluation
  • Regulatory impact assessment: analysis of a proposed regulation's benefits, costs and effects
  • Options matrix: comparison of policy options against explicit criteria
  • Transferability: whether a policy can work in a different context
  • Explanatory note: plain-language description of a bill's purpose and effects

📖 References

  • OECD — Regulatory Impact Assessment best practice principles.
  • Bardach, E. & Patashnik, E. A Practical Guide for Policy Analysis: The Eightfold Path to More Effective Problem Solving.
  • World Bank — Global Indicators of Regulatory Governance.
  • Cartwright, N. & Hardie, J. (2012). Evidence-Based Policy: A Practical Guide to Doing It Better.

quiz.q: An AI-drafted policy brief states that 'youth unemployment in the region is 38%'. No source is given. What should the analyst do?
opts: Use the figure as it seems plausible
Trace the figure to a verifiable source such as the national statistics institute, or remove it
quiz.x: Every statistic in policy work must be verifiable.

quiz.q: AI suggests copying a successful Scandinavian digital ID policy. What is the MOST important next step?
opts: Verify it in primary sources and assess transferability to local institutions, capacity and context
Ask AI whether it will work
quiz.x: Context differences determine whether policies transfer.

quiz.q: Which options analysis is MOST complete?
opts: Options chosen by political preference only
Several realistic options, including the status quo, assessed against explicit criteria with trade-offs
A list of every possible policy
One preferred option with supporting arguments
quiz.x: Good advice compares realistic options transparently.

quiz.q: A government plans a new regulation on informal transport. Which process analyses its benefits, costs and distributional effects before adoption?
quiz.x: RIA assesses expected impacts and involves consultation.

quiz.q: AI translates a bill from French to English for a bilingual legislature. What is required?
opts: Publish the AI translation as official
Qualified review to ensure both versions are consistent and legally equivalent
quiz.x: Both language versions carry legal weight in bilingual systems.

quiz.q: An analyst asks AI only for arguments supporting the minister's preferred option. What risk does this create?
opts: Biased analysis that misses evidence and counter-arguments
quiz.x: Balanced analysis requires seeking strongest arguments on all sides.

quiz.q: Which task requires qualified legislative drafters rather than AI alone?
opts: Drafting precise statutory text consistent with the constitution and existing law
quiz.x: Legal precision and consistency require expert drafters.

quiz.q: A ministry uses AI to simulate stakeholder views instead of consulting affected communities. What is the MAIN problem?
opts: Genuine consultation, especially of marginalised groups, cannot be replaced by simulation
quiz.x: Simulated views may miss real concerns and undermine legitimacy.

quiz.q: Which stage of the policy cycle examines whether a policy achieved its objectives?
quiz.x: Evaluation assesses outcomes and lessons.

quiz.q: Evidence contradicts a policy favoured by the government. What is the public analyst's duty?
opts: Delay the report until after decisions
Present the evidence honestly with its implications
quiz.x: Public service integrity requires honest presentation of evidence.

modules.d: Clear, accessible, truthful communication and casework with citizens — with transparency about AI.
modules.body:
Communication is a public service

Citizens need clear, accurate information to access services, understand decisions and participate in public life. Elected representatives receive large volumes of constituent enquiries; government agencies must explain complex policies to diverse audiences. AI can help draft, simplify, translate and organise communication — making public communication faster and more accessible — provided accuracy, honesty and privacy are protected.

Plain language and accessibility

Plain language means people can find what they need, understand it and act on it the first time they read it. AI can rewrite official text at an accessible reading level, structure information with headings and steps, and create versions for different audiences — while experts check that meaning has not changed. Accessibility also includes formats for people with disabilities (screen-reader-friendly documents, captions, audio, sign language where possible) and materials in the languages people actually speak. In multilingual countries such as Cameroon — with English, French and many national languages — translation quality must be checked by fluent speakers.

Truthfulness standard. Public communication must not mislead. AI can make messages more persuasive and polished, but persuasion must rest on accurate facts. Never use AI to fabricate statistics, quotes, endorsements or images presented as real. Corrections should be prompt and visible when errors occur.

Casework and constituent services

Representatives and their staff handle requests about benefits, documents, local services and grievances. AI can help categorise incoming messages, draft acknowledgements, summarise cases, and produce first drafts of responses or letters to agencies. Safeguards: constituent data is personal and often sensitive — use approved tools with appropriate data protection; staff review every response; and complex or urgent cases (safety, health, legal deadlines) are prioritised for human attention.

Government chatbots and digital assistants

Public-service chatbots can answer common questions at any hour. Good practice: tell users they are interacting with an automated system; ground answers in current, authoritative official information; state limitations clearly; provide easy routes to human help; avoid collecting unnecessary personal data; log and review answers for accuracy; and update content when laws or procedures change. A chatbot that confidently gives wrong legal or benefits information can harm citizens and expose the institution to liability.

Crisis communication

During emergencies — floods, disease outbreaks, security incidents — speed matters, but accuracy matters more. AI can help draft templates in advance, translate updates quickly and summarise incoming public questions. Messages should be verified, consistent across channels, coordinated with responsible authorities and tested for clarity.

Listening at scale

AI can analyse large volumes of public feedback — consultation responses, social media comments, call-centre logs — to identify themes and emerging concerns. Treat such analysis with care: online voices may not represent the whole population, and analysis must respect privacy and avoid profiling individuals for their political opinions.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my public communication assistant. I will paste an official notice or policy text. Rewrite it in plain language for the general public, keeping the meaning identical and listing any points where simplification might change meaning. Produce versions for social media and SMS, and flag what must be translated and checked by fluent speakers. Then draft a short FAQ answering the five questions citizens are most likely to ask.

📚 Glossary

  • Plain language: communication people understand and can act on the first time
  • Casework: handling individual constituents' requests and problems
  • Grounding: basing chatbot answers on authoritative sources
  • Profiling: automated evaluation of personal characteristics, including political opinions

📖 References

  • OECD — Good practice principles for public communication responses to mis- and disinformation.
  • PLAIN (Plain Language Association International) and plainlanguage.gov guidelines.
  • W3C — Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2.
  • UK Government Digital Service — content design guidance.

quiz.q: An AI rewrite of a tax notice makes it much easier to read but changes 'must file by 31 March' to 'should file around March'. What should happen?
opts: Correct it — simplification must not change legal meaning
quiz.x: Plain language must preserve exact obligations and deadlines.

quiz.q: A government chatbot answers benefit questions. Which practice is MOST important?
opts: Telling users it is automated, grounding answers in current official information and providing routes to human help
Making it sound human without disclosure
Collecting full personal details from every user
quiz.x: Transparency, accuracy and human escalation protect citizens.

quiz.q: A representative's office wants to paste constituents' health and family problems into a free public AI tool to draft replies. What is the issue?
opts: Sensitive personal data requires approved tools with appropriate protections
quiz.x: Constituent data is personal and often sensitive.

quiz.q: A campaign of public information uses an AI-generated photo of 'a local family' presented as real. What standard is violated?
opts: Truthfulness — synthetic images must not be presented as real
quiz.x: Fabricated images presented as real mislead the public.

quiz.q: During a flood emergency, which practice BEST balances speed and accuracy?
opts: Publish AI drafts immediately without checks
Use pre-prepared templates, verify facts with responsible authorities and keep messages consistent across channels
quiz.x: Preparation plus verification enables fast, accurate crisis communication.

quiz.q: Analysis of social media comments shows strong opposition to a policy. What caution applies?
opts: Online comments always represent the population
Online voices may not represent the whole population; combine with other evidence
quiz.x: Social media samples can be unrepresentative; profiling individuals raises privacy concerns.

quiz.q: Which accessibility measure helps deaf citizens follow a televised announcement?
quiz.x: Captions and sign language improve access for deaf people.

quiz.q: An official notice is translated into a national language by AI. What should happen before publication?
opts: Have fluent speakers check accuracy and clarity
quiz.x: Fluent review ensures meaning is preserved.

quiz.q: A published statistic in a ministry press release is found to be wrong. What should the ministry do?
quiz.x: Prompt visible corrections preserve trust.

quiz.q: Which casework should be prioritised for immediate human attention?
opts: Cases involving safety, health or imminent legal deadlines
quiz.x: Urgent, high-stakes cases need human handling.

modules.d: Ethical, lawful use of AI in campaigns, advocacy and civic mobilisation.
modules.body:
AI in campaigns: efficiency and responsibility

Campaigns and advocacy organisations use AI to draft speeches and messages, segment audiences, translate materials, plan events, coordinate volunteers, analyse polling and draft fundraising appeals. These uses can make smaller campaigns more competitive. They also raise serious risks: deceptive content, privacy violations, manipulation and breaches of election law. Responsible campaigns win trust as well as votes.

Know the rules

Election and campaign laws differ by country and change frequently. They may govern campaign finance, spending limits, disclosure of sponsorship, silence periods before voting, use of state resources, voter data and political advertising. Increasingly, laws address AI and synthetic media in political content. The European Union's regulation on transparency and targeting of political advertising imposes labelling and transparency requirements and restricts targeting using sensitive personal data; several U.S. states have enacted laws requiring disclosure of, or restricting, deceptive AI-generated election content; and electoral management bodies in many countries issue codes of conduct. In Cameroon and elsewhere, follow the electoral code and the guidance of the electoral authority. When uncertain, seek legal advice before launching AI-generated content.

Red lines for ethical campaigns. ① No deepfakes or synthetic content depicting real people saying or doing things they did not. ② No fabricated endorsements, quotes or statistics. ③ No deceptive impersonation of officials, election bodies or opponents. ④ No content designed to suppress voting or mislead people about when, where or how to vote. ⑤ Clear disclosure of AI-generated content where required by law or platform policy, and as good practice.

Voter data and privacy

Political opinions are sensitive personal data under many data protection laws. Collect only what you need, with a lawful basis; secure it; respect individuals' rights; and do not buy or use data obtained unlawfully. AI-driven microtargeting that exploits psychological vulnerabilities or sensitive characteristics raises legal and ethical concerns, as shown by the Cambridge Analytica controversy.

Legitimate high-value uses

  • Drafting and translating policy explainers in multiple languages.
  • Producing speeches and talking points from the candidate's or organisation's own positions.
  • Summarising polling and research into briefings.
  • Planning field operations and volunteer schedules.
  • Drafting accessible materials for people with disabilities.
  • Monitoring public conversation for misinformation about your campaign.
  • Testing message clarity with diverse audiences.

Advocacy and civil society campaigns

Advocacy organisations use AI to analyse legislation, draft petitions and submissions, mobilise supporters and tell stories of affected people. The same ethical standards apply: truthful claims, consent for personal stories, transparency about funding and authorship, and respect for opponents' dignity.

Fundraising communications

AI can personalise fundraising appeals, but avoid manipulative urgency and false claims, comply with donation rules (sources, limits and reporting), and honour unsubscribe requests and data protection rights.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my campaign compliance and communications advisor. I will describe my campaign or advocacy goal and country. Help me identify the legal rules I must verify (finance, advertising, data, AI disclosure, silence periods), draft a code of conduct for AI use with clear red lines, and produce three message drafts based only on the positions and facts I provide — flagging anything that needs verification or disclosure.

📚 Glossary

  • Microtargeting: tailoring messages to small audience segments using personal data
  • Voter suppression: efforts to discourage or prevent eligible people from voting
  • Silence period: pre-election period restricting campaigning in some countries
  • Disclosure: labelling AI-generated or sponsored political content

📖 References

  • European Union — Regulation (EU) 2024/900 on the transparency and targeting of political advertising.
  • International IDEA — resources on electoral integrity and AI.
  • U.K. Information Commissioner's Office — guidance on political campaigning and data protection.
  • National electoral codes and electoral management body guidance (verify for your country).

quiz.q: A campaign volunteer creates an AI audio clip of an opponent appearing to admit corruption, intending to post it as 'satire' without labelling. What is the BEST response?
opts: Post it on a secondary account
Refuse — deceptive synthetic content depicting real people is a red line and may be unlawful
quiz.x: Unlabelled deepfakes of real people mislead voters and may violate law.

quiz.q: An AI-generated SMS tells supporters of a rival party that voting has been moved to the following day. What is this?
opts: Voter suppression and deception, likely unlawful
quiz.x: Misleading people about when or how to vote is voter suppression.

quiz.q: A campaign wants to buy a dataset of citizens' religious affiliations and political opinions from an unknown vendor. What is the MAIN concern?
opts: Sensitive personal data may be unlawfully obtained and used, violating data protection law
quiz.x: Political and religious data are sensitive; lawful basis and source matter.

quiz.q: Which use of AI in a campaign is legitimate and low risk?
opts: Translating the candidate's own policy explainers into several languages with fluent review
quiz.x: Translating genuine positions with review is beneficial.

quiz.q: A campaign operates in a country whose law requires labelling AI-generated political ads. What must it do?
opts: Comply with the labelling requirement for all covered content
Avoid AI only on election day
quiz.x: Legal disclosure requirements must be followed.

quiz.q: What did the Cambridge Analytica controversy MOST highlight?
opts: Risks of using personal data obtained without proper consent for political profiling and targeting
quiz.x: It raised concerns over data misuse and psychological targeting.

quiz.q: An advocacy group wants to share the story of a woman affected by a policy. What is required?
opts: Her informed consent and accurate representation
quiz.x: Consent and accuracy are essential for personal stories.

quiz.q: A fundraising email drafted by AI says 'Last chance — campaign will shut down tonight' when this is false. What is the issue?
quiz.x: Fundraising must be truthful.

quiz.q: When unsure whether AI-generated content complies with election law, what should a campaign do?
quiz.x: Legal advice prevents violations.

quiz.q: Which practice reflects respect for opponents' dignity in advocacy?
opts: Arguing on evidence and positions without fabrication or personal attacks
Using AI to create humiliating fake images
quiz.x: Ethical advocacy contests ideas truthfully.

modules.d: Detecting, prebunking and responding to disinformation and synthetic media.
modules.body:
The threat

Disinformation — false information spread deliberately to deceive — threatens elections, public health, social cohesion and trust. Generative AI lowers the cost of producing persuasive false text, images, audio and video at scale. Notable cases include fabricated audio of a party leader released days before Slovakia's 2023 election, during a pre-election period when media coverage was restricted, and AI-generated robocalls imitating U.S. President Biden's voice to discourage New Hampshire primary voters in 2024, for which the political consultant behind them faced a multimillion-dollar FCC fine and criminal charges.

Distinguish the terms

Misinformation is false information shared without intent to deceive. Disinformation is false information spread deliberately. Malinformation is genuine information shared to cause harm, such as leaked private data. Responses differ: correcting a well-meaning misinformed citizen differs from countering a coordinated influence operation.

Verification skills

  • Source check: who published it first? Is the account new, anonymous or impersonating someone?
  • Reverse image and video search: tools such as Google Lens, TinEye and the InVID-WeVerify plugin help find earlier versions or original contexts of images and video frames.
  • Context check: is a real image being reused from another event, date or place?
  • Lateral reading: open new tabs to see what reliable sources say about the claim and the source, rather than analysing the page itself.
  • Signs of synthetic media: inconsistencies in lighting, hands, text, lip-sync or audio artefacts — though detection by eye is increasingly unreliable.
  • Provenance: content credentials based on the C2PA standard can show how content was created and edited, where publishers adopt them.
Detection tools are not verdicts. AI-detection tools for synthetic text, images and audio produce both false positives and false negatives. Use them as one signal among several — source, context, corroboration and provenance — not as proof.

Prebunking and resilience

Research on inoculation theory by Sander van der Linden, Jon Roozenbeek and colleagues shows that exposing people in advance to weakened forms of manipulation techniques — emotional language, false dichotomies, scapegoating, fake experts — improves their ability to recognise them later. Prebunking campaigns, including large-scale tests with short videos on social platforms, have shown measurable effects. Media literacy, trusted local messengers and transparent institutions build long-term resilience.

Responding effectively

  1. Assess reach and harm before responding; responding to a fringe falsehood can amplify it.
  2. Verify facts quickly with authoritative sources.
  3. Respond with the truth first — the "truth sandwich": state the fact, briefly note the falsehood, and repeat the fact.
  4. Use trusted messengers and the channels where the falsehood spreads, including WhatsApp and local languages.
  5. Report coordinated or illegal content to platforms and authorities.
  6. Document incidents for analysis and accountability.

Using AI defensively

AI can monitor public conversation for emerging narratives, cluster similar claims, draft fact-check explainers and translate corrections into multiple languages quickly. Human fact-checkers verify and decide. Respect free expression: counter falsehoods with truth and transparency rather than suppressing legitimate dissent.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my disinformation response coach. I will describe a claim, image or video circulating in my community (without personal data). Guide me through source, context and provenance checks and suggest verification tools to use. Help me decide whether and how to respond given its reach, and draft a truth-sandwich correction for WhatsApp in plain language, marking facts I must verify with authoritative sources.

📚 Glossary

  • Disinformation: false information spread deliberately
  • Misinformation: false information shared without intent to deceive
  • Prebunking: pre-emptive exposure to manipulation techniques
  • Lateral reading: checking a source by consulting other sources
  • C2PA: standard for content provenance and credentials
  • Truth sandwich: fact, brief mention of falsehood, fact again

📖 References

  • van der Linden, S. (2023). Foolproof: Why Misinformation Infects Our Minds and How to Build Immunity.
  • Roozenbeek, J. et al. (2022). Psychological inoculation improves resilience against misinformation on social media. Science Advances.
  • Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) — c2pa.org.
  • FCC (2024) enforcement action regarding AI-generated robocalls in the New Hampshire primary.
  • Wardle, C. & Derakhshan, H. (2017). Information Disorder. Council of Europe.

quiz.q: A viral photo claims to show flooding in your city today. Reverse image search finds the same photo from another country in 2019. What is this?
opts: Real content reused out of context
quiz.x: Genuine images reused with false context are a common form of misinformation.

quiz.q: An AI detector says a video is '92% likely real'. What is the BEST interpretation?
opts: One signal among others — combine with source, context, corroboration and provenance
quiz.x: Detectors produce errors; they are not verdicts.

quiz.q: A false rumour about vaccines circulates in a small WhatsApp group with little reach. What does the course advise considering first?
opts: Assessing reach and harm, since responding widely may amplify it
Immediately issuing a national press release
quiz.x: Response should be proportionate to avoid amplification.

quiz.q: Which correction structure is recommended?
opts: Repeat the false claim prominently and then deny it
Truth sandwich: fact, brief mention of falsehood, fact again
quiz.x: Leading and ending with truth reduces reinforcement of the falsehood.

quiz.q: What does inoculation (prebunking) research show?
opts: Exposing people to weakened manipulation techniques in advance improves their recognition of manipulation
quiz.x: Prebunking builds resilience before exposure.

quiz.q: Fabricated audio of a party leader emerges two days before an election during a media silence period. Which case does this resemble?
quiz.x: Slovakia's 2023 election saw a deepfake audio released in the final days.

quiz.q: A citizen shares false information believing it is true. Which term applies?
quiz.x: Misinformation lacks intent to deceive.

quiz.q: Which practice is lateral reading?
opts: Reading the suspicious page very carefully from top to bottom
Opening other reliable sources to check what they say about the claim and the source
quiz.x: Professional fact-checkers verify by leaving the page to consult others.

quiz.q: How can AI help a fact-checking team responsibly?
opts: Deciding what is true without human review
Monitoring emerging narratives, clustering claims and drafting translated corrections for human verification
quiz.x: AI accelerates monitoring and drafting; humans verify and decide.

quiz.q: Which standard helps show how a piece of digital content was created and edited?
quiz.x: C2PA provides provenance information where adopted.

modules.d: A practical playbook for responsible AI use in your institution, campaign or civic organisation.
modules.body:
Your civic AI playbook

Your capstone is a Civic AI Playbook for a government unit, legislature office, political campaign, party or civil society organisation. It should enable effective AI use while protecting citizens' rights, trust and democratic integrity.

Playbook components

  1. Context: organisation, mandate, audiences, jurisdiction and applicable laws (data protection, electoral, public administration, AI regulation).
  2. Principles: legality, accountability, transparency, equality, privacy, participation and truthfulness.
  3. Approved uses: priority use cases — for example policy research, plain-language communication, translation, casework drafting, consultation analysis, misinformation monitoring.
  4. Prohibited uses and red lines: deceptive synthetic media, fabricated claims, voter suppression, unlawful profiling, automated decisions about citizens without legal basis and human review.
  5. Data rules: handling of citizens', constituents' and voters' data; approved tools; sensitive data protections.
  6. Verification and review: sources for every fact; human review before publication; correction procedures.
  7. Transparency: when and how AI use is disclosed to the public.
  8. Disinformation response plan: monitoring, verification, response thresholds, truth-sandwich templates, trusted messengers, reporting channels.
  9. Roles and accountability: who approves uses, reviews outputs and responds to incidents.
  10. Training and review: staff training and a review schedule as laws and tools change.
Legitimacy test. For each use in your playbook, ask: if the public learned exactly how we used AI here, would it increase or decrease trust in our institution or campaign? Uses that would decrease trust need redesign or removal.

Your capstone deliverable

Submit the playbook (no more than six pages), a disinformation response template, and one worked example applying the playbook to a real or realistic scenario. Your mentor reviews it for legality, non-partisanship, practicality and democratic integrity.

  • Legitimacy test: whether full public knowledge of an AI use would increase or decrease trust
